content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In mainstream Christian teaching the net most commonly symbolizes the gospel and the kingdom of God as an instrument for gathering people: the work of evangelism by which souls are drawn into the church. This flows from Jesus' call to make his disciples 'fishers of men' and from the parable of the dragnet, where the net cast into the sea gathers fish of every kind, representing the kingdom's ingathering of all peoples pending final separation of righteous and wicked at judgment.","primary_basis":["Matthew 4:18-20 (fishermen casting a net called to be fishers of men)","Mark 1:16-18","Matthew 13:47-50 (parable of the dragnet: 'the kingdom of heaven is like a net')","Luke 5:1-11 (miraculous catch of fish; 'from now on you will catch men')","John 21:1-11 (post-resurrection catch of 153 fish, net not torn)"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"A snare or trap laid by the wicked, by enemies, or by seductive persons—symbolizing hidden danger, plots, and entrapment in sin or death, from which the righteous pray for deliverance.","basis":["Psalm 9:15","Psalm 10:9","Psalm 25:15","Psalm 31:4","Psalm 35:7-8","Psalm 57:6","Psalm 140:5","Psalm 141:9-10","Proverbs 1:17","Proverbs 29:5","Ecclesiastes 7:26","Micah 7:2"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"An instrument of divine judgment: God spreading his net over nations or rulers to capture them for punishment or exile.","basis":["Ezekiel 12:13","Ezekiel 17:20","Ezekiel 32:3","Hosea 7:12","Lamentations 1:13","Job 19:6"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Oppressive human power or idolatrous self-reliance—Babylon 'catching men like fish in a net' and sacrificing to its own net—read as a symbol of predatory empire and worship of one's own strength.","basis":["Habakkuk 1:14-17"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"In patristic and later ecclesiological interpretation, the unbroken net of John 21 (with its 153 fish) symbolizes the unity and universality of the church, which holds all nations without schism; the tearing net of Luke 5 is sometimes contrasted as the church in the present mixed age.","basis":["John 21:11","Luke 5:6","interpretations in Jerome, Augustine (Tractates on John; sermons on the two catches of fish), and Gregory the Great"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"General entanglement in affliction or testing permitted by God ('you brought us into the net'), read devotionally as trials that refine the believer.","basis":["Psalm 66:10-12"],"prominence":"rare"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"The symbol is strongly context-dependent and carries a well-recognized dual valence: in New Testament and homiletic usage the net is overwhelmingly positive (gospel/kingdom gathering souls, evangelism), while in Old Testament poetry and prophecy it is predominantly negative (snare of the wicked or net of divine judgment). Christian teaching most often foregrounds the positive evangelistic sense because of the 'fishers of men' call and the dragnet parable, so that is treated here as the primary consensus meaning, with the trap/judgment senses as widely acknowledged secondary readings rather than fringe views."}
